Kesh counted the stairs down to the workshop. Forty-one. He always counted. His father had told him once that a man who counts keeps his hands honest, though his father had said a lot of things, and none of them had kept him alive.

Six years at the eighth forge and the wheel still knew his hands better than any person did. He sat, set the grindstone turning, and began the work that would, if the gods were fair and Master Oren was in a giving mood, make him a journeyman by the first snow.

Journeyman meant wages. Wages meant coins. Coins meant he could stand in front of Drego Culvane the week before Winterveil and buy his mother's debt down to nothing, or at least down to a number she could carry. Culvane wanted the house by spring. The paper said so. Kesh had read the paper forty-one times too, or close enough.

"Seventeen strikes per pass," Oren Vael said from behind him, in the voice he used for everything, the voice of a man pricing fish. "Sixteen if your wrist is good. Your wrist is not good."

"No, Master."

"So seventeen."

The wheel screamed against the billet. Sparks. Kesh counted the strikes under his breath. He'd been grinding these blades for a week straight. Eleven sabers, guild-standard, destined for the caravan guards on the southern pass. Honest work. Sold work. The eighth forge did not have much work these days that was either of those things.

The guild war had starved them. House Merrin's allies had squeezed the third-rate smiths off every good contract in Vhalun for two years, and Kesh knew exactly which family had starved his forge, because it was the same family that had bought his father's contract off the guild when the worksite collapsed and the compensation claim came due. Nine coppers owed on a dead man. House Merrin had paid the nine coppers, then sold the debt to a collector, then bought the mountain where the collapse happened. Kesh had been nine years old. He kept a mental ledger too, though his was not meticulous.

At midday the delivery cart came. Kesh heard it on the cobbles and went to the door, because the cart was supposed to carry their steel order and they were three weeks short on billets.

The cart was carrying crates out.

Eight of them, long, heavy, the weight distributed wrong for billets and right for something finished. Two porters Kesh had never seen were loading them, and Tam Breel, the forge's bookkeeper, stood by with his arms crossed, looking anywhere except at Kesh.

Kesh wiped his hands and bent to look at the nearest crate. Oak slats, iron banding, and on the end panel, stenciled in white:

IX-M.

Guild-style seal. Clean work. The ninth forge's mark, in format, if not in letter. The ninth forge had gone cold two months ago, everyone in Vhalun knew it, the master smith dead, apprentices scattered, the guild council still arguing over the lease. Nothing had shipped from the ninth forge since midsummer.

"We're running their freight?" Kesh asked.

Tam Breel examined the sky. "We're running freight."

"Whose freight?"

"Freight that's paid for." Tam flicked two fingers. Porters lifted. The cart creaked away toward the eastern dock road, toward House Merrin's warehouses, and Kesh watched it go the whole way down the hill.

Oren Vael came out of the office, drying his hands on his apron.

He glanced at the cart the way a man glances at weather.

"Heavy crates," Kesh said. "Wrong weight for billets."

"Mm." Oren looked at him. Oren's eyes were pale gray and they weighed things the way his scales weighed things, and when they weighed Kesh they usually took a second longer than Kesh liked. "You've got nine blades left. Nine. Finish them and your evaluation piece can come from the same batch. Best of the nine, and we submit it."

"Master, about the evaluation. My mother's debt—"

"Is a number." Oren turned back toward the office. "I deal in numbers. Bring me a good blade and we will discuss numbers."

It was more than Kesh had gotten from him in months. It should have been enough. It was almost enough.

Then Tam Breel carried the quarterly account ledger past him, open, on his way to file it, and Kesh, who had spent six years learning to read numbers the way other men read faces, caught the coal column as it went by.

Double.

The eighth forge had bought double coal this quarter. Kesh knew, because he ordered it, because he stacked it, and because he fed the forges himself six days out of seven. He had fed no more coal than last quarter. He had fired no more blades. Output was down, way down, three contracts gutted since spring.

He did the arithmetic standing in the doorway with his scarred hands hanging at his sides. If you bought double the coal and produced the same steel, the extra heat had gone somewhere. Heat was the one thing a forge could not hide. Heat was money burning.

That night he waited until Oren left. The old man locked the office, took the lamp, said, "Nine blades, boy," and climbed the forty-one stairs, counting under his breath too. Kesh had never told him he'd noticed that, and never would.

Kesh stayed. Banked the fires. Then he went to the coal bay and counted.

Sacks in: he counted them twice. Forty more than the ledger said he'd burned. There was no room in the bay for forty sacks of steel nobody had made. There was no slag. There was no scale-cake on the flues.

A forge that burns coal makes ash, and the eighth forge's ash pile had not grown since summer.

Which meant the coal was burning somewhere else.

He walked the workshop floor slow, lamp down, and he did not know what he was looking for until he found the quench barrel, the big one, iron-hooped, against the east wall, and saw the chalk behind it. Faint. Scrubbed at, mostly gone, but the top line was fresh, redrawn maybe yesterday.

Tallies. Shift tallies. Somebody kept a count of something back here, behind the barrel, where an apprentice hauling water wouldn't look twice. Nine strokes, a space, nine strokes, a space, four. And under it, in Tam Breel's cramped hand: M.

House Merrin.

Kesh stood very still. The banked fire ticked behind him. He thought: if the ninth forge's seal is on crates leaving this shop, and Merrin's letter is on the chalk behind our own quench barrel, then the ninth forge is not cold. It moved. It moved into the eighth forge, in the dark, and my master is feeding it.

He thought about the evaluation. He thought about Culvane holding the debt paper and smiling with his small teeth. He thought: one word to the wrong person and Oren Vael does not submit my blade, does not discuss numbers, and the house is gone before the thaw. He thought: my father worked for a guild that paid nine coppers for his life and I am six weeks from kneeling in front of the same kind of men, asking them to let my mother keep her roof.

Nobody else was going to count this. Tam knew and looked at the sky. The porters came from outside. Only Kesh stood between the chalk and the truth, because only Kesh needed the truth this badly.

He wet his thumb, reached past the barrel, and before he could stop himself he copied the tallies onto his own palm in lamp-black. Then he blew out the lamp, climbed the forty-one stairs, and stopped at the office door with his hand on the latch, where the first ledger lived in the locked drawer, and where, if a man like Oren Vael kept meticulous books, there might be a second one.

He put his shoulder to the door.
